The post Creative higher education is part of our national infrastructure, but without a plan, it is being set adrift appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Roni Brown, Chair of the Creative HE Strategy Project and Professor Paul Fieldsend-Danks, Chair of GuildHE Creative.

This country has a world-leading creative industries sector. It also has world-leading creative higher education institutions, and the first is inextricably linked to the second. The creative industries contributed £145.8bn in gross value added in 2024, 5.5 per cent of the UK economy, and has grown by 19.7 per cent since 2019 against only 4.4 per cent for the economy as a whole (DCMS). Skills England also identifies them as the largest high-growth employment sector. Three-quarters of the creative workforce holds a degree, compared with around half of the UK workforce overall.

That is not a coincidence. Our colleges, art schools, conservatoires and higher education institutions develop the ideas, technique, enterprise skills and adaptability that creative careers demand. They also supply the studios, theatres, galleries, facilities and equipment that support students to learn and make a place culturally and economically alive, with more than 4.2 million public visitors last year to higher education art spaces. In addition, employers worldwide place a high premium on creative capabilities, and according to the World Economic Forum’s 2025 global employer survey, creative thinking stands as the fourth most sought-after core skill. Therefore, these skills are not just vital to the creative industries, but to the health of our businesses across the whole economy both at home and abroad.

An ecosystem under pressure

However, sustained financial pressures across higher education and cultural sectors threaten essential infrastructure. Declining public funding across teaching and research budgets forces higher education providers to close creative courses and spaces, reducing graduate numbers in a number of creative disciplines and stripping communities of vital cultural hubs. This loss weakens the UK by eroding infrastructure that fosters place, social cohesion and innovation. Unchecked, this decline harms one of the UK’s greatest assets and will impede progress on the Government’s Industrial Strategy.

Why a strategy, and why now?

Recognising that persistent arguments about the value of creative higher education have failed to yield sustained policy or funding support, GuildHE committed to developing a strategic framework to unify arguments for government, regulators, industry, and higher education providers and create a single vision for the sector.

Currently open for consultation, this draft framework outlines a long-term mission, vision and enablers to build a resilient creative higher education sector that supercharges impact.

Developed over the last 18 months with insights from more than 150 organisations, the GuildHE Creative Consortium, a 22-member taskforce spanning government, industry, and education, and independent evidence analysis by Counterculture, it is crafted in tandem with the Creative Education Coalition and its updated manifesto by translating a vision of a strong creative higher education sector into practical interventions across funding, regulation and policy to secure it.

The mission and vision

Our mission is to unleash the full potential of creative higher education by securing policies, funding, and activity to enable it to power sustainable economic growth and secure the UK’s cultural prosperity into the future.

To advance this mission, we’ve outlined three strategic visions for the future of creative higher education:

Creative higher education is recognised as critical civic infrastructure that powers place-based development and growth, including civic participation, regional prosperity and local pride.

A pioneering creative-practice research and innovation ecosystem is sustained and its unique value as an indispensable driver of the UK’s cultural leadership, economic growth and ability to solve 21st-century challenges is recognised through targeted investment and regulatory parity.

An agile creative education system is integrated with industry and community to power growth, social mobility, and societal wellbeing.

These visions define our ambitions and guide our upcoming work with stakeholders. Key recommendations focus on strengthening regional and national partnerships, improving impact measurement, and establishing a creative industries skills pact. Rather than calling for substantial new financial investment, the framework focuses on strategic alignment to fully realise existing capacity.

We have provided examples throughout this document and on the GuildHE website of the work which informs this framework, along with insights gathered from higher education providers, industry leaders, sector bodies, and policymakers and case studies. These will be updated as the project progresses.

What next

We are delighted to receive feedback on this draft framework from across higher education providers, cultural organisations, industry partners, and the wider public. Please submit your consultation responses via this link by 12 January 2027.

title: Schools given emergency action plans for power outages and extreme weather
summary: Cyber attacks and building collapses are among the risks schools in England are being urged to prepare for.
full_text:
Schools in England have been told to prepare for emergencies including national power outages and water shortages under updated government guidance.

New action cards, which provide practical steps for staff to take during an incident, have been issued to schools for the first time to help them respond immediately.

Loss of connectivity, cyber attack, environmental hazards and extreme weather are all listed as possible incidents that could seriously disrupt education.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) said schools "already strive to remain open in emergency situations and only take the decision to close where there is no alternative option".

The union said schools and colleges have robust emergency plans and procedures in place which are regularly reviewed and updated.

The updated guidance, external for all education and childcare settings follows lessons learned from recent events, including wildfires and cyber attacks.

The Department for Education says the cards, external should form part of every school's existing emergency planning and staff training.

The guidance says closing schools would not necessarily reduce the risk to children and young people, as the same emergency may also affect their homes or the wider community.

"Remaining at the setting may sometimes be the safer option," it says.

Head teachers are being asked to consider how long their schools could remain open if critical services were disrupted, including overnight.

The guidance says plans should show how they would support anyone unable to be collected or who needed to remain on site overnight.

They should also set out how they would obtain water, food and essential medical supplies if deliveries were disrupted.

Schools should also refer to the National Risk Register, which sets out the most significant risks facing the UK, when planning for emergencies, the guidance says.

Earlier this year, the government warned that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households needed to have enough supplies to last three days as part of its "Be Ready" campaign.

The cards cover what to do in the event of flooding, heatwaves, health incidents such as infectious disease outbreaks, utility disruptions and security-related events.

They also include advice on dealing with suspicious drone activity, hoax threats and smoke from wildfires.

In the event of a national power outage, for example, the advice includes filling up "potable water supplies", using fresh food first and preparing for wider community use if requested.

If a school were to lose all connectivity, including online services and telephone lines, the guidance says it should confirm how it would contact 999 and use paper registers where necessary.

The government says further action cards may be added in the future.

It also says they should be accessible during disruptions to power, connectivity or digital systems.

Universities and higher education providers are expected to apply the guidance proportionately too.

Tom Middlehurst, from ASCL, said incidents like this summer's "intense heatwaves" - which led to hundreds of schools either fully or partially closing - "happen very quickly and entail having to make decisions and communicate them to families and staff at pace".

He said schools' "number one priority at all times" was the safety and wellbeing of students and staff, adding that it was "not particularly helpful" of the government to "lecture them about the importance of staying open".

title: Despite political divide, Americans often 'speak in one voice'
summary: In this era of sharp American divide, politics has increasingly become a dish families work to keep off the Thanksgiving table. But in reality, data show Americans actually agree on many tough topics, spanning more than 100 policies. Lisa Desjardins spoke with two leading researchers whose counter-intuitive findings suggest our division is based on politics, not policy.
full_text:
Lisa Desjardins:

In this era of sharp American divide, politics has increasingly become a dish families work to keep off the Thanksgiving table. But, in reality, data show Americans actually agree on many tough topics spanning more than 100 policies.

Earlier this week, I spoke with two leading researchers whose counterintuitive findings suggest our division is based on politics, not policy.

Steven Kull directs the Program for Public Consultation at the University of Maryland, whose recent surveys have identified dozens of policies with widespread political agreement. And Tatishe Nteta is a professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of the UMass Poll. He focuses on public opinion, race, and political behavior.

Welcome.

Steven, let me start with you.

How much do we agree, and how?

Steven Kull:

Well, something that Americans really agree on is that they're not being listened to. And they believe that, if Congress would listen to the people more, they would find more common ground.

And we have done a lot of research on this, and it turns out basically the public is right, that there is a tremendous amount of bipartisan common ground among the American people on a wide range of issues. They do disagree about candidates, they do disagree about parties, but when it comes to public policy, there's a huge amount of issues that they do agree on.

Lisa Desjardins:

Tatishe, do you agree? Do we agree much?

Tatishe Nteta:

The story is that Americans can't agree on much of anything.

But I agree with Steven that, if you sort of dig down into the data, you do find these areas of uniformity and agreement. And our poll data also has shown this as well. On issues like AI, on issues like corruption and the pessimistic view of the economy, Americans really do speak in one voice.

Lisa Desjardins:

Let's talk about immigration. I can imagine some viewers bracing themselves. This is a common sharp divide.

But, Steven, I'm going to start back with you again. You actually found some very specific policies where there's broad agreement on what to do.

Steven Kull:

Yes.

There is bipartisan agreement that we should deport criminals. But when it comes to people who have been here for a while who are not criminals -- and that's most immigrants, undocumented immigrants -- there's an agreement that they should be given a path to legal status, provided they pay their back taxes and a penalty, but they should be able to stay here.

There's also agreement that employers should check to see that people have legal status. But there's also support for having more work visas so that there are more ways for people to come here legally to meet the demand for workers.

Lisa Desjardins:

Tatishe, what about big tech?

Tatishe Nteta:

Yes, there's clear consensus on Americans' distaste for the construction of AI data centers in their local communities.

You look at Republicans and Democrats and independents, you look across racial groups, class groups, generational groups, majorities of Americans overwhelmingly oppose the construction of these AI data centers and view very little in the way of material benefits to their communities or to themselves specifically, and really just see high levels of cost, whether that's environmental or higher cost in terms of the utilities that they're paying with the construction of these data centers.

And I think that's a reflection of a growing distaste for the AI industry more generally.

Steven Kull:

And I'd like to add to that. There's also support for having a federal agency regulate artificial intelligence, particularly when it comes to making critical decisions like who gets health insurance or who gets hired.

There's also very strong support for regulating the use of deepfakes, particularly in political campaigns.

Lisa Desjardins:

All right, let's continue undaunted into these issues that in Washington seem so hard, a big important one, health care.

Tatishe, you and I were talking about the American dream. You talk to your class about that. Where do you see agreement on health care?

Tatishe Nteta:

This is another area where I think Americans, as I said, speak in one voice, that their -- the amount of money that they are paying for their health insurance and the precarity of that health insurance coverage continues to be a problem, even in a sort of post-Obamacare America.

And they are desirous of the federal government and even their state governments to do something about this particular issue.

Lisa Desjardins:

Steven, that's the problem, but you found Americans also agree on some of the solutions or at least the policy they want.

Steven Kull:

Yes, that's right.

There's support for the government getting involved with health insurance more, providing access to Medicare for 55-to-64-year-olds, and in general offering a public option. There's support for the government getting more involved in trying to regulate drug pricing. There's opposition to reducing Medicaid spending. In fact, there's even support for increasing Medicaid spending.

So there's -- yes, there are a whole range of options that would really -- would make a difference in terms of the cost of health care.

Lisa Desjardins:

So out of this whole conversation, I have a bigger question. Where do we get this narrative that Americans are hopelessly divided?

Tatishe Nteta:

I think the narrative begins when you look at institutions like the U.S. Congress, which are rife with high levels of conflict, partisan conflict.

I think you get this narrative if you spend too much time on social media, which feeds us a lot of information and news which emphasizes conflict.

Lisa Desjardins:

Steven.

Steven Kull:

Americans believe that there is actually more common ground among the people than there is in the political system. And they're annoyed by it.

Now, does that mean they don't get pulled into it? Do they get worked up on this issue or that issue? Sure. And the candidates actively work people up and try to focus on areas where there is division to get -- to get people juiced up.

Look, if we would just calm down a bit and really consult the people, we would be able to move through many of these conflicts and solve many of the problems that we face today.

Tatishe Nteta:

And I can add to that one of the things that is consistent is that Americans really want this upcoming Congress to work together, to go across partisan lines, to go across ideological lines, and to find those areas of agreement that we do see in public opinion and that we do see on Main Street.

Lisa Desjardins:

We are going to have divided government in January. Are you optimistic that not just Americans, but politicians in Washington can find more agreement?

Steven Kull:

I can't say I'm terribly optimistic. There is a lot of investment in these kinds of polarized positions, and there are a lot of special interests that do prod them to take these positions.

But they always have that option to orient more to the people. And if they do, the public is going to respond positively to that, and they're going to move toward solving some of these problems.

Lisa Desjardins:

Tatishe.

Tatishe Nteta:

I'm actually optimistic.

I think one of the stories that are coming out of this past midterm election is that Americans want real solutions to the economic challenges that they face. Their support of the Democratic Party over Republican incumbents consistently across different electoral offices says that there needs to be some movement on this particular issue, or that the American people will speak again in one voice and remove those individuals who are in power today until they can find those that can address this issue.

Lisa Desjardins:

Steven Kull and Tatishe Nteta, thank you for an excellent conversation. Happy Thanksgiving to you both.

Tatishe Nteta:

Thank you so much. Same to you.

Steven Kull:

Happy Thanksgiving. Thank you.

title: This Independent is giving Poilievre's Conservatives the jitters ahead of a crucial byelection
summary: The federal riding of Brantford-Brant South has been a Conservative stronghold for most of the last 20 years. But an insurgent Independent candidate who was passed over by leader Pierre Poilievre is trying to stop Tory rule in an upcoming byelection — and there are early signs he's gaining traction.
full_text:
The federal riding of Brantford-Brant South has been a Conservative stronghold for most of the last 20 years. But an insurgent Independent candidate who was passed over by leader Pierre Poilievre is trying to stop Tory rule in an upcoming byelection — and there are early signs he's gaining traction.

That candidate is Dave Carrol, a pastor at Freedom House — a big church with a long list of parishioners — and a local media personality with regular segments on Rogers TV.

Those positions, plus his decades of advocacy on issues like homelessness, and his "Captain Kindness" superhero persona at community events like the Santa Claus parade, have made him a known quantity in this mid-sized industrial city in Ontario's southwest.

With endorsements from past Conservative MPs in the area, including Phil McColeman and the outgoing Larry Brock, Carrol sought the party's nomination for the Dec. 7 vote.

But he never had the chance to test his support among the party faithful. Poilievre unilaterally appointed ex-mayor Kevin Davis as the candidate, upsetting Carrol and his supporters who thought he was best placed to keep the seat for the blue team. The party has since revoked his membership.

After being snubbed, Carrol struck out on his own, cobbling together the campaign team and resources needed to take on the Liberal-Conservative duopoly in this area.

If the election sign war is any indication, Carrol is poised to do better than most independents who vie for a seat in the House of Commons.

Parts of the city are blanketed with Carrol signs emblazoned with his campaign slogan: "People first. Community always."

In some neighbourhoods, the Carrol signs easily outnumber the Conservative ones.

In an interview with CBC News, one of his first with a national news organization since his Conservative candidacy went awry, Carrol said this campaign is not about getting even with Poilievre.

"I've spent most of my adult life dressed up in a Captain Kindness costume, walking around talking about how to use kindness to transform a community. What I'm doing has absolutely nothing to do with revenge," he said.

But he said the party's move to block his candidacy and usurp the will of some local Conservative members did inspire him to jump into the fray.

'Not a revenge vote'

"We are frustrated with this decline in democracy," Carrol said.

"But this has not been a personal endeavour. This is not a revenge vote. This is not a protest vote. This is a purposeful choice to put people's voices at the forefront."

And so far, he said, the reception has been "tremendous," as his message of tackling the scourge of homelessness and addiction has resonated in a part of the province hit hard by both.

Still, he's cognizant of what a victory could mean for Poilievre and the Conservatives.

"There's a national spotlight because this is a consequential election," he said. "The people I talk to are not nervous, they're excited."

But some federal Conservatives are feeling skittish.

This particular byelection has the potential to be hugely consequential for Poilievre given it's the one riding out of the six up for grabs that is most likely to change hands next month, according to a recent survey by Abacus Data. Brock won the seat by about 11 percentage points in the last federal election but Conservative support nationally has fallen off since then.

Poilievre has been a frequent presence in the riding this fall, often giving up his weekends to door-knock in a seat that could decide his fate.

There have been six federal byelections so far this year and the Conservatives have lost them all. Party sources told CBC News that if the Conservatives fall short in Brantford, it could ignite a movement to oust Poilievre as leader as some MPs grow restless after a prolonged losing streak.

One Conservative source described Brantford as Poilievre's "Toronto-St. Paul's moment," a reference to the 2024 Liberal byelection loss in a party stronghold that was the beginning of the end for former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill this week, Conservative MP Ben Lobb said this election could be a nail-biter.

"I don't think anybody knows how that is actually going to go," Lobb said. "I think everybody would say it's close. So really, on that one, it's whoever gets out the vote."

Poilievre, meanwhile, has bristled at questions about what this Brantford byelection could mean for his tenure at the top.

"You all ask this question again and again and again over the last several days," Poilievre said at a news conference this week.

"I think we actually have to focus in the byelections on the simple questions: Can you afford your groceries more today than when Mark Carney became prime minister? Or is it time to lower costs with a Conservative approach?" he said.

While Liberal candidate Joy O'Donnell, a local businessperson, is a serious contender for the seat given the party's recent strength in national polls, the Conservatives have so far focused their negative campaign messaging on Carrol.

In some homes across Brantford, voters have received direct mail from the Conservatives with a warning of what they say could happen: "A vote for Dave Carrol is a vote for the Liberals."

Carrol said he's not splitting the Conservative vote, claiming he's drawing support from voters of all political stripes who are tired of a party-dominated, "Ottawa knows best" approach.

"We have people who have not just voted for, but served across the political spectrum," he said.

Carrol's Conservative opponent, was not available for an interview.

"As he approaches the final stretch of the campaign, Kevin is prioritizing his time at the doors, connecting directly with voters," a party spokesperson said of Davis.

Carrol doesn't have access to the sophisticated voter databases used by the big parties to track supporters and turn them out.

But there's a steady stream of campaign volunteers through Carrol's quaint office that he's taken to calling his "campaign cottage," given its rustic nature compared to the relatively more comfortable digs of Davis's strip mall election outpost just a few blocks away.

The campaign is doing things the old-fashioned way, sending its committed roster of volunteers out with a map and a clipboard to collect the names and phone numbers of potential Carrol supporters.

While it's always an uphill battle as an Independent, Carrol said voters in this part of the Ontario heartland have a recent history of eschewing party politics and backing an independent candidate with deep roots in the community.

Ontario MPP Bobbi Ann Brady from the neighbouring Haldimand-Norfolk riding has a similar story. A longtime community advocate, she was passed over for the PC nomination when the party appointed a candidate and then ran as an Independent. Brady has since won the seat twice, with huge margins.

"I am fired up because I genuinely care about this. For me, this is not about politics. It's about people," Carrol said.

"And so do I think we have a chance of winning this? I absolutely do."

title: Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?
summary: The presumptive House speaker's political pragmatism will be tested by divisions over healthcare, Israel and Iran.
full_text:
The overwhelming blue wave of the 2026 United States midterm elections should have simply been seen as a crowning achievement for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries that propelled him into the position of next speaker of the House of Representatives. And while that outcome appears all but guaranteed now that he has secured more than enough support from the incoming House Democratic Caucus, Jeffries’ ascent to the top House leadership position has been significantly rockier than anticipated.

The blue wave was, in part, a progressive and anti-establishment phenomenon. And while we in the media have likely exaggerated the impact of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in this year’s election cycle, DSA-affiliated and other newly elected far-left lawmakers have already asserted themselves as a vocal minority amongst the incoming House Democratic Caucus. They’ve done so by calling on the party to move left on issues such as healthcare, campaign finance and America’s relationship with Israel. And these newly elected progressives have also targeted congressional leaders, namely Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who they see as embodying the party’s status quo.

Jeffries has reached the pinnacle of power within his party by being a shrewd political operator who has deftly managed the leverage of the Democratic minority in the closely divided House. His handling of the recent challenge to his leadership shows that he remains a step ahead of his opponents within the party. Jeffries declined the opportunity to be chosen by acclamation, an option that could have allowed him to gloss over the opposition to his speakership. Instead, Jeffries insisted on a formal secret ballot. The choice was strategic. Much like a prime minister calling for early elections, he organised the vote to happen before progressive opposition had coalesced around a single candidate (unlike in the Senate, where Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen is amassing support to challenge Schumer). The move represented a tactic Jeffries observed while under the wing of Nancy Pelosi, who called a similar vote in 2018 after her leadership was challenged by vocal incoming members of Congress. In the end, potential challengers for the role of speaker, such as Representatives Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, declined to throw their hats in the ring to run against Jeffries. The vast majority of the caucus fell in line behind the New York congressman, with 251 votes in favour and only 11 against, the latter largely from incoming DSA-aligned representatives-elect.

For Jeffries, the progressive revolt against his leadership has been, in the short term, a mere speed bump on his path to becoming speaker. In the longer term, those 11 “no” votes represent a more significant progressive challenge to Jeffries’ record and agenda that will not easily disappear. However, the presumptive next speaker of the House is poised to overcome this challenge, as his skill as a political operative, the relatively weak position of his progressive opposition, and the historic nature of Jeffries’ leadership all work in his favour.

Over the course of the 2026 election cycle, Jeffries secured the support of important progressive figures, including fellow New Yorkers such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. During the brief post-election speculation over his leadership, the New York congressman also won over progressives including Texas Representative Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Jeffries’ predecessor as Democratic leader, Pelosi, was able to manage dissent from the progressive Squad through a combination of personal relationships and strategic committee assignments that channelled their energies toward oversight of the executive branch. Jeffries may likewise seek to manage the “Bloc”, as the new progressives are being called by some, in similar fashion.

Meanwhile, Jeffries’ primary message since the midterm elections has been one of affordability, a potent message that has resonated with voters across the political spectrum and thus can unite centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party. The speaker-designate has also signalled that he is willing to move in the direction of progressives’ concerns on substantive issues. Most notably, on November 17, the eve of the speaker nomination vote, Jeffries endorsed a plan to expand Medicare by lowering the age of eligibility for older Americans, covering children under 18, and including dental, vision and hearing coverage. This new “Medicare for more” plan, coupled with rolling back Trump-era cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits, has been gaining steam among both centrists and progressives. The latter have framed it as a quickly achievable first step towards Medicare for All. Both progressive elder statesman Senator Bernie Sanders and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus have adopted this rhetoric.

Whether this “first step” framing is accurate is unknowable. The Affordable Care Act was presented in similar terms, but the progressive aim to use Obamacare as a foundation to build a universal healthcare system did not materialise over the subsequent decade. However, the willingness of major progressive forces to adopt the narrative seems to be opening space for Jeffries to navigate. This undercuts the power that the incoming progressives have to make healthcare a major dividing issue within the Democratic caucus.

Jeffries also has the power of history on his side. The congressman from Brooklyn is poised to take control of the top House spot as the chamber’s first Black speaker. He will be backed by an unprecedented slate of diverse leaders within the Democratic House Caucus, with historic firsts for Black, Hispanic and Asian legislators, among others. Even President Donald Trump acknowledged Jeffries’ personal acumen and the historic nature of becoming the first Black speaker, calling it “a big deal”, and referring to Jeffries as “a very smart guy”. Jeffries has in turn signalled a willingness to work with members of the Trump administration, though not with new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, who Jeffries calls a “stone-cold racist”.

Black candidates and Black voters played huge roles in Democrats’ 2026 surge in ways that have not neatly mapped onto the “centrist insiders v. progressive outsiders” narrative that has defined the party’s main internal division. Though Black Democrats and progressives are by no means mutually exclusive wings of the party, the far left has sometimes had difficulties appealing to Black voters. As such, progressives face potential backlash if they are perceived as attempting to prevent or hamstring the leadership of the first Black speaker of the House. Already, some of the attacks against Jeffries have been condemned for racist language and undertones. Progressives run the risk of being tone-deaf and appearing on the wrong side of history, meaning that they will have to tread lightly if they continue to question Jeffries’ leadership.

In the short run, Jeffries has made the right moves politically and leaned into the importance of the moment, all while solidifying his coalition and moving leftward in a way that balances progressive priorities with legislative practicality. Whether he can temper progressive demands and maintain a unified caucus may depend on forces outside of his control. In terms of Democrats’ domestic agenda, incoming Senate sensation and Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is becoming the face of the Medicare for All movement, even pushing for a long-shot deal with President Trump on the issue. Growing momentum within the Senate could push the issue beyond Jeffries’ ability to manage. Similarly, in a recent New York Times interview, Jeffries signalled a willingness to walk a tightrope between holding the Trump administration accountable and working with the White House and other Republicans. But this balancing act may prove untenable if the continued lawlessness of Trump and his cabinet leads to intensified demands for investigations and even impeachments.

And foreign affairs may be an even larger stumbling block for Jeffries, who has come under fire for his support for Israel as sentiment grows in both parties to re-evaluate the US relationship with its longtime Middle East ally. For now, Jeffries has gotten some cover by gaining the support of figures like Mamdani, a vocal and credible critic of the genocidal war in Gaza and of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians. But in that same New York Times interview, Jeffries prevaricated when asked about accepting AIPAC funding in the future or pushing for legislation that would cut weapons sales to Israel and impose sanctions on entities tied to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Again, Jeffries appears to be offering a compromise, promoting the less forceful West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act, which targets the sponsors of settler pogroms but not the underlying scheme of settlement itself in Palestinian territory. It’s less clear that such a stance will be enough to satisfy Jeffries’ left flank. However, the growing controversy over AIPAC led the pro-Israel lobbying group, even prior to November’s election results, to shift its strategy of supporting candidates to a model that emphasises individual donors rather than direct political action committee funding for campaigns. The electoral shellacking that AIPAC-backed candidates experienced in the midterm elections may further lead the lobbying organisation to take a less high-profile approach going forward, which could help to slightly tone down Israel’s prominence in US politics.

For the time being, the Iran war is the more pressing foreign policy concern, and this will be one of Jeffries’ first major tests. He has pledged to prioritise ending the war, a popular stance that could be another unifying position for centrists, progressives and even some Republican lawmakers. But the speaker-designate has already been criticised for indicating that he might be willing to cut a temporary budget deal with Republicans that keeps money flowing to the war rather than using the leverage of a government shutdown to insist on cutting funds for the conflict. Even Trump and Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged the Iran war as a major reason behind Republicans’ 2026 defeats. Failure by Jeffries to take bold action against the conflict now will be seen as a missed opportunity and create a new opening for progressives to question his fitness to lead in this moment.

After securing the nomination for speaker, Jeffries surprised the incoming Democratic House caucus with a visit by former President Barack Obama, to whom Jeffries has been compared before. Obama was a unique leader who combined a principled pragmatism with an unmatched ability to inspire, and he urged the new Democratic representatives to stick to their principles while learning how to “get s*** done” with colleagues who had different points of view. Jeffries leans more toward Obama’s pragmatism than his idealism, and his penchant for practicality at the expense of vision may be the presumptive speaker’s greatest strength and biggest liability. Even if he is willing to compromise with the left wing of his party, Jeffries will not be the bold visionary that progressives want leading the House. But with domestic and foreign concerns to address such as healthcare and the war with Iran, Jeffries has the chance to be the leader who gets things done. Jeffries will have the next two years to accomplish these and other goals for the party and its supporters. Whether or not he delivers results on these issues, and how voters assess the party’s performance come 2028, will make or break Jeffries’ speakership.

title: Private markets are more accessible than ever for investors. Getting out is another matter
summary: Retail access to private markets is growing, but PwC says education lags as redemption limits put liquidity risks in focus.
full_text:
Retail investors are lining up to back private funds. But education on how restrictive these funds can be, particularly on when and how much money they can get back, may not be keeping pace with the influx of new capital.

PwC research has found that 77% of fund distributors surveyed said access to private markets is becoming important or very important to what they plan to offer clients, but just 15% of asset managers said they provide comprehensive education for retail investors.

Unlike the public markets retail investors are more used to, some private-market vehicles limit when investors can get their money back to set repurchase windows, and even then may return only part of what they request.

Why liquidity matters

A spike in redemption requests at several private-credit funds earlier this year exposed the tension between giving investors regular opportunities to cash out and holding assets that can be difficult to sell quickly.

Blackstone restricted withdrawals from its $79 billion flagship nontraded BCRED private credit fund to 5% of shares in June, after redemption requests hit 10% during the second quarter. Apollo also capped withdrawals in its Apollo Debt Solutions vehicle at 5% after second-quarter redemption requests surged to almost 17%. Blue Owl , Morgan Stanley and Partners Group also limited investor withdrawals from some of their funds.

watch now

Limitations on redemptions are a key trade-off in structures such as LTAFs in the U.K., ELTIFs in the EU and interval funds in the U.S., which broaden access to less-liquid assets.

It's emerged as a major pressure point as those structures come under closer scrutiny.

"Private markets can have very different characteristics from the products many wealth clients are used to, particularly around liquidity, valuations and holding periods," said Albertha Charles, global asset and wealth management leader at PwC.

"Investors and advisers need to understand how these products work, including their liquidity and valuation characteristics, so they can make informed decisions about whether they are appropriate."

PwC's 2026 Asset Management Revolution report, published Nov. 23, surveyed 250 asset managers, 100 institutional investors and 100 distributors across 36 countries and regions. More than half of respondents represented firms with over $20 billion in assets under management.

Among the study's key findings, education and liquidity are seen as the main hurdles as private markets reach a broader investor base. Distributors said better advisor and client education would help expand access, while liquidity, lock-ups and suitability requirements remain major barriers. Private equity and private credit were also the areas where distributors saw some of the biggest gaps in advisor knowledge.

Private credit appears likely to draw the strongest demand — two-thirds (66%) of distributors expect it to lead client interest in private markets, compared with 46% for private equity.

Routes to access

Regulators in several major markets are creating structures to widen access to long-term and illiquid assets. The U.K. uses long-term asset funds, or LTAFs, while the EU's European long-term investment funds, known as ELTIFs, can be marketed across member states.

watch now

In the U.S., interval funds provide periodic, rather than daily, liquidity. Singapore, Japan and Hong Kong have also taken steps to broaden retail or listed access to private assets. The frameworks differ, but all aim to make less-liquid investments workable within existing distribution, suitability and liquidity requirements.

Yen Sum, global chair of the private capital practice at Latham & Watkins, and a member of its executive committee, said access to private-market funds is generally limited to investors who certify they are qualified or sophisticated.

She told CNBC on Thursday that the key issue for investor education centers on how private assets differ in liquidity, maturities and return-of-capital terms, and how higher rates can pressure leveraged companies — rather than simply whether regulation should curb access.

title: Australia faces challenging 2027 as early international student figures emerge
summary:
Australia’s international education sector is facing another challenging year in 2027, with early recruitment figures emerging amid ongoing concerns over student visa approvals.

The post Australia faces challenging 2027 as early international student figures emerge appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
As of November 20, 44,900 prospective international students held active student visas against the government’s 2027 planning level of 295,000 new international student commencements.

As previously reported by The PIE News, the Australian government announced in July that it would maintain its National Planning Level (NPL) at 295,000 for 2027.

However, government data as of November 6 showed that the sector had reached 83% of its 2026 allocation, with public universities reaching just 67%, compared with 150% among other higher education providers.

“Contrary to sector hopes that the federal government would make good on its 295,000 commencements in 2026, we are likely to only achieve 250,000 in total,” Phil Honeywood, chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), told The PIE.

“This will provide the government with a good headline to counter the Opposition and One Nation parties attack on overseas student numbers.”

Australia’s NPL is used to manage international student growth through a visa prioritisation system rather than a hard enrolment cap.

Under Ministerial Direction 115, offshore student visa applications face lower processing priority when a provider reaches 80% of its indicative allocation, with a third priority tier kicking in at 115%.

While public universities have collectively reached almost 19% of their 2027 allocations and all remain at Priority 1, eight other higher education providers are already at Priority 2 and three are listed at Priority 3.

Honeywood also anticipates a decline in onshore transfers in 2027, pointing to the planned introduction of a new transfer visa from July.

“Onshore transfers have propped up the private higher education providers who argue that the NPL methodology as applied to them, for offshore recruitment, has been discriminatory,” he said.

The figures come amid wider concerns over student visa refusal rates in key source markets, with the Australian government recently consulting on proposed changes to its student visa settings.

Notwithstanding debate around the NPL, all providers are genuinely concerned about the massive decline in student visa approvals

Phil Honeywood, IEAA

“Notwithstanding debate around the NPL, all providers are genuinely concerned about the massive decline in student visa approvals,” said Honeywood.

“While the government claims it is addressing this through, for example, potential changes to financial capability evidence, any such reforms will take significant time to implement.”

“All in all, with few political friends, 2027 is shaping up to be another incredibly challenging year for Australia’s beleaguered international education sector.”

title: Is Your Class Worth It?: Connecting Classes to Workforce Skills
summary:
It’s no secret that college tuition is rising rapidly causing students to rethink the value of a college degree and consider alternative paths to a career. But they might also question the value of your class and wonder if it is worth their money, time, and effort. How will your class help them meet their […]

The post Is Your Class Worth It?: Connecting Classes to Workforce Skills appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
It’s no secret that college tuition is rising rapidly causing students to rethink the value of a college degree and consider alternative paths to a career. But they might also question the value of your class and wonder if it is worth their money, time, and effort. How will your class help them meet their career goals and improve their job skills? Addressing those questions in course planning and design can yield impressive results including increased focus and motivation, a positive effect on students’ approach to assignments, and changing viewpoints on homework assignments as valuable learning experiences.

These outcomes can be achieved with three simple steps: a first day discussion, homework that asks students to read about classroom skills in action and reflect on how they will use the same skills in their careers, and TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) assignments that show students the purpose for homework and/or major assignments.

1. The First Day Discussion

Instead of starting class with introductions or discussing the syllabus, start by asking students how they think your class will help them. In my freshman English classes I ask, “Why do you think NSU requires this class? Why do you think it might be important?” Prompt them to brainstorm why the class is part of their degree program. What skills will they learn that will help them in other classes, their lives, and careers? Write the answers on the board or type them and project them onto a screen. Put added emphasis on career skills learned and give examples of how they will be used.

For example, in my English course I might mention using narrative writing skills when preparing an accident report for a police officer or a client progress report for a physical therapist or using argument essay skills to write a proposal for new equipment at work.

2. Homework About Skills In Action

Use interviews or case studies of the skills in action in the workplace for each unit. In my English 1010 course I have students read an interview with a working professional discussing narrative writing, evaluations, and argument essay skills and how they use them on the job. Once students read the interviews, I ask them to write one or two paragraphs discussing how they will use this skill or skills in their daily lives, in classes, and/or in their future careers.

Good interviews are provided in The McGraw Hill Guide, 5th edition and Business Communication Today, 16th edition. Interviews are also available online or a guest speaker could be invited to the class.

If you only have time to make one change, this one generated the most positive feedback on student surveys.

3. TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) Assignments

TILTed assignments are constructed around a Purpose, Task, and Criteria. I reworked each major assignment in my freshman English classes to meet the TILTed framework for Spring 2026, focusing especially on the purpose section. This strongly connects the writing task with the reasons for doing it such as meeting objectives of the class and future workforce duties.

For example, for a narrative writing assignment, the purpose was as follows: “This assignment eases you into the types of academic writing expected in a college setting while also letting you express yourself creatively by writing your own story. It helps you meet the goals and objectives of the class by demonstrating writing as a purpose-driven process of communication and demonstrating writing to diverse audiences, for a specific purpose, in a specific context. It also enhances skills needed for the workplace where narrative is part of many different writing tasks such as writing an incident report for a police officer, writing a patient progress report for a physical therapist, or writing a pupil progress report as a teacher.

More information about TILTed assignments is available at https://www.tilthighered.com/resources or https://www.uwidocs.org/2020/03/31/tilt-your-assignment-prompts/.

Results—What Did Students Think?

Throughout the Spring 2026 semester, through talking to students and grading homework submissions, I knew the new framework was helpful, but I also gathered data for the TILTed versus unTILTed assignments in my online literature course and the overall framework using all three moves in my freshman English courses. Students were given a Microsoft Forms survey to complete with extra credit points given for participation.

When rating the workforce skills homework assignments where they read an interview with a working professional discussing using the learned skills and then reflected on how they would use them in their own lives, 81% of the students said the homework helped them see the essays “as a valuable learning experience rather than just ‘busy’ work.”

Further, 95% of students said the homework assignments helped them to understand the relevance of each essay type for their future careers.

Ranking from 1 to 5, with 5 being the highest level, students ranked reflecting on the practical applications of these essay types as affecting their focus and motivation while writing the essays at a 4.24 level overall. Since focus and motivation are often lacking in English courses, I was happy to see such positive results in this area.

Students were also asked “if the homework assignments about workplace skills helped you improve focus and motivation when writing the essays, explain how and why.”

Among the more positive comments were, “[It] helped me see a point to the writing,” “It allowed me to put in perspective how important it is to learn how to write correctly and how I will use this in my future career,” and “When doing these homeworks they were not just busy work they were a way to help reflect on what we would be doing and how we should go about writing these essays in an appropriate way.”

Students were also asked how the homework assignments about workplace writing impacted their approach to the assignments. Among comments were, “The homework assignments about workplace writing helped me approach the class assignments with a more practical mindset. Instead of seeing each task as just another school requirement, I started thinking about how the skills could translate into real communication I might use in a job—like organizing information clearly, choosing the right tone, and writing with a specific audience in mind. Understanding how writing functions in professional settings made me pay more attention to clarity, purpose, and conciseness in my essays. It also helped me realize that the techniques we practice in class aren’t just academic—they’re tools I’ll actually need in the workplace.”

Another student wrote,” It made me more careful about what I was writing and honestly made me more passionate. Those smaller writing assignments concerning the workplace made me remember that writing isn’t just a temporary thing and it is a valuable skill to know.” Yet another reflected, “These assignments about the workplace impacted my approach to them because I was more interested in talking about something I wanted to do in the future.”

In a separate survey, students in my sophomore required literature course viewed both the TILTed and unTILTed versions of two major assignments. Results showed 75% preferred the TILTed version. Overall, they felt the TILTed version was more specific, gave examples, and answered more questions students might have. Some liked the TILT format of showing the purpose, task, and criteria better; and most students said the TILTed versions were more transparent and clearer overall when specifically asked to comment on that aspect.

On an even more positive note, 75% said the TILTed assignments increased their motivation.

And those are the reasons I’m doubling down on these strategies for future courses.

If you have comments or ideas for other techniques to increase connections to workforce skills, let me know in the comments.

Stephanie Reese Masson is an instructor of English, social media manager, and department internship coordinator at Northwestern State University of Louisiana. Her work has appeared in Prime Number Magazine, Word Catalyst, Peacock Journal, and The Battered Suitcase. She has authored academic articles for the MERLOT Journal of Online Learning and Teaching, The Chronicle of Higher Education, and Louisiana English Journal.

title: Authenticity in teaching: common ground or a lost cause?
summary: by Stacey Mottershaw and Michael Reynolds The language of authenticity has become increasingly prominent across higher education. We hear about authentic assessment, authentic learning and authentic engagement. Yet authenticity is also frequently positioned as a route to enhancing student belonging, … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Stacey Mottershaw and Michael Reynolds

The language of authenticity has become increasingly prominent across higher education. We hear about authentic assessment, authentic learning and authentic engagement. Yet authenticity is also frequently positioned as a route to enhancing student belonging, helping students to feel recognised, valued and connected within their university communities (Gravett and Winstone, 2020). Despite growing enthusiasm for authenticity in higher education, an important question remains: do staff and students actually mean the same thing when they talk about authentic teaching?

Our research explored perceptions of authenticity amongst staff and students at the University of Leeds. Through a series of focus groups, we examined how participants understood authenticity, whether they considered it important, and what they saw as its benefits and limitations. The findings revealed considerable common ground, but also some important differences.

What does authenticity mean?

Both staff and students described authenticity in remarkably similar ways. Across the focus groups, authenticity was associated with being genuine, honest and true to oneself. Participants frequently connected authenticity with integrity, sincerity and consistency between values and actions.

Students described authenticity as “being yourself without exaggerating” and “not being pretentious”. Staff similarly talked about authenticity as honesty and being able to “be yourself”, albeit within professional boundaries. At first glance, this signals broad agreement. However, our findings echo earlier work suggesting that while staff and students both value authenticity, they do not necessarily interpret or prioritise it in the same way (Kreber & Klampfleitner, 2013).

Students: authenticity is helpful, but content comes first

Student participants generally valued authenticity in teaching. They appreciated lecturers who shared relevant experiences, demonstrated passion for their subject and appeared approachable and human.

Authenticity helped students to trust their lecturers, and made learning feel more engaging. Several participants highlighted the importance of seeing lecturers as real people, rather than distant authority figures. Authenticity could make asking questions feel easier and contribute to a more inclusive learning environment.

Students consistently drew boundaries about what they considered to be useful in the realm of authenticity. For many, authenticity was a welcome addition to teaching but should not be a central educational goal. Personal stories, opinions and experiences were valued when they enhanced understanding of the subject. When they perceived it to not enhance the subject then students became more sceptical.

A recurring message from the student focus groups was simple: authenticity should not reduce time spent on teaching content. As one participant put it, students come to university primarily to gain knowledge. Authenticity was seen as beneficial when it enriched learning, but problematic when it distracted from it.

Staff: authenticity is complex

Staff focus groups revealed a much more complicated relationship with authenticity. While staff also saw authenticity as being true to oneself, they frequently emphasised its limits, tensions and risks. Authenticity was rarely discussed as an unrestricted expression of identity. Instead, it was framed as something negotiated within professional, institutional and social constraints, echoing arguments that authenticity involves values, relationships and responsibilities as well as self-expression (Kreber et al, 2007).

Participants regularly used language such as “boundaries”. One member of staff described authenticity as being able to be oneself, but only within the constraints of a particular situation. Another linked authenticity directly to psychological safety, suggesting that the extent to which staff can be authentic depends on whether they feel safe enough to do so. Several staff members suggested that authenticity became easier as their careers progressed, mirroring earlier observations that academic identities evolve over time (Archer, 2008).

This contrast between students and staff perhaps mirrors their different life and professional experiences. Many students appeared to approach authenticity as an uncomplicated ideal limited only by the boundaries of time. Staff see complexity, as they see authenticity as a nexus of evolving professional identity, organisational expectations and responsibility. It is worth noting that staff cared deeply about authenticity. For many, it was far more than a teaching technique; it was connected to questions of identity, values and professional integrity.

Authenticity as a form of connection

One of the most interesting differences between the two groups concerned the relationship between authenticity and connection. Students tended to describe authenticity as something that helped them to connect with lecturers, making staff seem more approachable, trustworthy and relatable, whilst staff often saw connection as the purpose of authenticity. Being authentic was not primarily about self-expression, but instead it is a way of building relationships, creating trust and encouraging students to engage more fully with their learning.

Several participants across both groups suggested that authentic teaching creates space for students to be authentic themselves. In this sense, authenticity was seen as reciprocal. By modelling openness, honesty and vulnerability, staff hoped to foster similar qualities amongst their students. Yet they also recognised the potential tensions. For example, one participant reflected on situations where both staff and students were being authentic, but where competing perspectives required compromise to avoid harming group learning. Authenticity, therefore, is not always straightforwardly positive.

Who gets to be authentic?

The findings also highlighted the uneven nature of authenticity within higher education. Staff participants acknowledged that authenticity may be easier for some colleagues than others. Factors such as race, class, gender, accent, nationality, neurodiversity and career stage can shape whether educators feel able to bring their authentic selves into the workplace. Some described feeling pressure earlier in their careers to conform to be an “identikit lecturer”. Others discussed adapting aspects of their identity to fit professional expectations.

These reflections remind us that authenticity is not simply an individual choice. It is shaped by organisational cultures, disciplinary norms and broader social structures. Calls for greater authenticity in teaching therefore need to account for the varying degrees of risk and vulnerability experienced by different members of academic communities.

What can we learn from this?

Our findings suggest that staff and students value authenticity, but not always in the same way.

Students generally regard authenticity as a positive feature of teaching that can support engagement and connection. However, they place clear limits on its importance and remain primarily focused on the quality of learning and pace of content delivery. Meanwhile staff often experience authenticity as a more complex and professional concern. Their reflections reveal additional labour in the form of an ongoing negotiation between personal values, professional responsibilities and institutional expectations.

Perhaps the most important takeaway is that authenticity cannot and should not be treated as an unquestioned good. Authentic teaching matters not because it involves unrestricted self-expression, but because it can help to create meaningful educational relationships that supports learning. The challenge for educators is not simply to be authentic, but to consider how, when and for whom authenticity enhances learning.

In an era where belonging and connection have become central concerns for higher education, authenticity may indeed have an important role to play. But our research suggests that its value lies less in revealing the self and more in creating the conditions for productive, trusting and inclusive educational relationships.

Dr Stacey Mottershaw is an Associate Professor (Teaching and Scholarship) in the Management and Organisations Department at the University of Leeds. Her research seeks to understand the needs of under-represented groups in higher education, focusing on equitable and socially just career development.

Dr Mike Reynolds is an Associate Professor (Teaching and Scholarship) in the Economics Department at the University of Leeds. His research is focused on improving teaching and outcomes in Higher Education.

title: Ante las amenazas de la inteligencia artificial y las presiones financieras sobre la publicación académica
summary:
Carta de las Editoriales Universitarias

La entrada Ante las amenazas de la inteligencia artificial y las presiones financieras sobre la publicación académica se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
Declaración conjunta – 11 de noviembre de 2026

La Carta de las Editoriales Universitarias (University Press Charter) reúne por primera vez a las editoriales universitarias en torno a un compromiso común para construir un futuro mejor para la publicación académica, en un momento en el que la confianza, la calidad y el aprovechamiento eficiente de los recursos públicos se encuentran amenazados.

Presentada durante la Semana de las Editoriales Universitarias (del 9 al 13 de noviembre de 2026), la Carta fue impulsada por siete editoriales universitarias, mediante una colaboración encabezada por Cambridge University Press y Bristol University Press. El documento establece la contribución singular que realizan las editoriales universitarias al conocimiento académico, la educación superior, la innovación y la sociedad.

Mandy Hill, directora general de Cambridge University Press, declaró:

«Las presiones sobre el ecosistema de la publicación académica son considerables. Están surgiendo riesgos reales a medida que se producen más artículos en menos tiempo, mientras algunas editoriales no dan prioridad a una revisión por pares rigurosa y, como consecuencia, disminuye la confianza generalizada en los contenidos. Algo tiene que cambiar.

»No es demasiado tarde para redefinir el futuro de la publicación académica. Seguir haciendo lo que siempre hemos hecho no será suficiente. Es fundamental que este cambio esté impulsado por las necesidades de los académicos, y las editoriales universitarias pueden desempeñar un papel crucial en este proceso. Es nuestra responsabilidad hacerlo».

Desde su difusión, 108 editoriales de 26 países se han adherido a la Carta. Asimismo, Les Éditions Universitaires de l’Afrique Centrale, la Associação Brasileira das Editoras Universitárias y University of Wales Press están preparando traducciones al francés, portugués y galés, respectivamente.

La Carta compromete a sus signatarios a anteponer la calidad y la integridad al volumen de contenidos, aumentar la transparencia sobre el valor y los costos de la publicación, mantener el juicio humano en el centro del uso de la inteligencia artificial (IA), ampliar el acceso equitativo al conocimiento y promover el reconocimiento justo de las contribuciones académicas a la publicación, como la revisión por pares.

Las editoriales universitarias —incluidas las editoriales institucionales, las gestionadas por bibliotecas y otras pertenecientes a universidades— se distinguen por su compromiso con el conocimiento académico y la educación, proporcionando una base para la innovación. Por lo general, cualquier excedente financiero se reinvierte en la actividad editorial y en la misión académica más amplia, en lugar de distribuirse entre accionistas privados.

title: “Democratizar el futuro”
summary:
El análisis de Pablo Vommaro en Cadena 3 sobre los sueños y desafíos de los jóvenes

La entrada “Democratizar el futuro” se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
En diálogo con Cadena 3, el director ejecutivo del Consejo Latinoamericano de Ciencias Sociales (CLACSO), Pablo Vommaro, reflexionó este miércoles sobre las conclusiones de su artículo “¿Qué futuro imaginan los jóvenes?”, publicado en Le Monde Diplomatique.

ESCUCHAR NOTA

El historiador, sociólogo e investigador de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (UBA) explicó que el trabajo surgió a partir de las indagaciones realizadas junto al Grupo de Estudios de Políticas y Juventudes, donde constataron un escenario marcado por la creciente precarización de las condiciones de vida y una acentuada desigualdad temporal.

Según indicó el especialista, la ruptura de una temporalidad lineal y secuencial ha dado paso a una dinámica efímera e inmediata, que dificulta la capacidad de las juventudes para proyectar el mañana con una mirada esperanzadora.

En ese marco, Vommaro advirtió sobre la debilitación de la histórica promesa intergeneracional en Argentina –sintetizada tradicionalmente en el anhelo del «hijo doctor»–, según la cual el esfuerzo presente garantizaba un bienestar superior para las camadas venideras.

Al diluirse esa certeza de progreso futuro, se produce un fenómeno de «presentificación» de las expectativas, donde los jóvenes buscan compensar el esfuerzo laboral cotidiano a través de satisfacciones inmediatas.

De este modo, los recursos se destinan a experiencias como viajes, recitales, consumo tecnológico o ayuda puntual a sus familias, postergando objetivos de largo plazo como el acceso a la vivienda propia o el ahorro para la jubilación.

Por otra parte, el investigador cuestionó el estigma que califica peyorativamente a la juventud como una «generación de cristal», aclarando que no se trata de fragilidad o debilidad emocional, sino de una postura ética que no tolera las violencias y malos tratos aceptados en el pasado.

El titular de CLACSO remarcó que las mujeres y varones jóvenes buscan vivir con mayor fidelidad hacia sus propios ideales en el día a día, rechazando el acoso laboral, el bullying y la violencia de género.

Asimismo, instó al mundo adulto a superar el «adultocentrismo» y cambiar la lógica comunicativa: en lugar de preguntarse cómo hablarles a los jóvenes, sugirió generar espacios genuinos de escucha activa y empatía para reconocer su protagonismo.

El especialista también alertó sobre las presiones de un contexto caracterizado por el hiperindividualismo y el hiperconsumismo, donde el éxito social suele medirse a través de la exhibición de bienes en plataformas como TikTok e Instagram.

Ante esta realidad, subrayó la urgencia de implementar políticas públicas concretas que intervengan en la cotidianeidad juvenil, como la articulación efectiva entre educación y trabajo para evitar que miles de estudiantes deban abandonar sus estudios por necesidades económicas.

Para Vommaro, el Estado debe acompañar la realidad de quienes enfrentan inserciones laborales precarias pero demandan un consumo real o aspiracional.

Finalmente, el sociólogo destacó la importancia de los espacios de congregación y pertenencia comunitaria donde las juventudes encuentran contención y bienestar colectivo.

Al abordar los desafíos que enfrentan la sociedad y las instituciones en la actualidad, Vommaro sintetizó en su artículo en Le Monde Diplomatique el núcleo fundamental de su planteo intelectual: «Quizá el desafío generacional de esta época consista en democratizar el futuro.»
